title: Vinted vs eBay: Which Is Better for Selling Clothes in the UK? (2026)
intro: Vinted and eBay are now both free to sell on for UK private sellers, so the old "Vinted is free, eBay charges fees" comparison no longer holds. This guide breaks down the real differences — fees, buyer protection, shipping, audience, and what actually sells on each — so you can pick the right platform for what you're selling.

body.heading: The short answer: both are now free, so fees aren't the decider
paragraphs: Until October 2024, the easy comparison was that Vinted charged sellers nothing while eBay took a 12.8% final value fee. That's no longer true. eBay UK now lets private sellers list and sell for free — 300 free listings a month, no final value fees — as long as you're a UK-based private seller and not using optional upgrades or delivering overseas.

Vinted still charges sellers nothing too, with the buyer paying a ~5% + £0.70 Buyer Protection fee. So for the typical UK private seller clearing out a wardrobe, the two platforms are now roughly equal on seller fees.
That means the real decision comes down to other factors: who's buying, how buyer protection works, how shipping is handled, and what kinds of items actually sell. This guide walks through each one.

body.heading: Seller fees compared side by side
paragraphs: Vinted: sellers pay £0 — no listing fee, no final value fee, no commission. The buyer pays Buyer Protection (~5% + £0.70) on top of their total, but the seller receives the full price they set.

eBay: free for UK private sellers — 300 free listings per month, no final value fee, no regulatory operating fee. Fees only apply if you list more than 300 items in a month (35p per extra listing), add optional upgrades (subtitle, reserve price, promoted listings), or deliver to an overseas address.

The practical difference: casual sellers on both platforms pay nothing. High-volume sellers and resellers will hit eBay's 300-listing cap and start paying, while Vinted stays free regardless of volume. For that reason, resellers who list in volume often prefer Vinted's zero-fee model — see [our guide to reselling on Vinted](/guides/reselling-on-vinted).

body.heading: Buyer protection: different models
paragraphs: Vinted builds buyer protection into every sale as a mandatory fee. If an item doesn't arrive, arrives damaged, or isn't as described, the buyer opens a claim and Vinted refunds them. It's uniform and automatic — read [how Vinted Buyer Protection works](/guides/vinted-buyer-protection) for the details.

eBay's equivalent is its Money Back Guarantee, which is free for buyers (no separate fee) and covers the same situations: not received, not as described, or damaged. The buyer's protection is comparable, but eBay's dispute process has more history and, in some buyers' eyes, more established resolution.

Both hold payment until delivery, and both side with buyers who provide good evidence. The difference is cost placement: on Vinted the buyer pays a small fee for it; on eBay the protection is built into the platform's economics without a visible buyer-facing fee.

body.heading: Shipping and postage
paragraphs: Vinted uses integrated shipping labels — you choose a package size when listing, and when it sells Vinted generates the label. Integrated shipping means lost or delayed parcels are handled through the courier with Vinted's support, which protects you as the seller. The buyer pays shipping, or you can offer it free.

eBay gives you more shipping flexibility: you choose the courier and service (Royal Mail, Evri, etc.), set your own postage price, and can offer collection or international shipping. That flexibility is useful for larger or higher-value items, but it also means more admin and less built-in protection if you arrange postage yourself.
For small, postable clothing items, Vinted's integrated labels are simpler. For bulky or high-value items where you want control over the courier, eBay's flexibility wins.

body.heading: Audience and what actually sells
paragraphs: Vinted's audience is younger and more budget-conscious, and the platform is built around second-hand fashion: clothing, footwear, accessories, and home. Buyers search by brand and browse catalogues. Fast fashion, branded high-street pieces, vintage, and premium denim all move well. If you're selling clothes, Vinted is arguably the more focused marketplace.

eBay's audience is broader and more general — it sells everything from electronics to car parts to collectibles, and buyers are often looking for specific items rather than browsing fashion. For clothing, eBay is strong on vintage, designer, and collectible pieces, but the fashion experience is less curated than Vinted's.

The rule of thumb: everyday and branded clothing sells better on Vinted; rare, collectible, or non-clothing items sell better on eBay. For more on what moves, see [what sells best on Vinted](/guides/vintage-denim-on-vinted) and our comparison of [Vinted vs Depop](/guides/vinted-vs-depop).

body.heading: Discoverability: searching vs browsing
paragraphs: Vinted is a browse-and-discover platform. Buyers scroll catalogues, follow sellers, and see recommendations, so even a small wardrobe can get views if the photos and titles are good. Saved searches and notifications are core to how serious buyers shop — which is why [Vinted alert tools](/guides/vinted-price-alert) exist.

eBay is a search-and-buy platform. Buyers type a specific query, and listings with strong titles, categories and item specifics win. There's less casual browsing and more intent-driven search, which suits buyers hunting for one particular thing.

The practical implication: on Vinted you optimise for visibility and engagement (photos, freshness, favourites); on eBay you optimise for search relevance and item specifics. The same item can need different treatment on each platform.

body.heading: Which should you choose?
paragraphs: Choose Vinted if you're selling clothing, footwear or accessories, want zero fees with no listing caps, prefer integrated shipping with built-in protection, and value a browse-heavy audience that shops by brand.

Choose eBay if you're selling non-clothing items, collectibles, electronics, or anything bulky or high-value where you want courier flexibility and an audience of intent-driven searchers. Its free-listing model for private sellers makes it genuinely competitive now.

Many serious sellers use both — cross-listing the same item doubles your reach, and the two audiences barely overlap. The main risk of cross-listing is selling the same item twice, so whatever you do, keep your inventory in sync.

Whichever you pick, the fundamentals are the same: good photos, specific descriptions, and researched pricing. Start with our [complete guide to selling on Vinted](/guides/how-to-sell-on-vinted) and apply the same discipline wherever you list.

faq.question: Is eBay still free to sell on in the UK?
faq.answer: Yes, for UK-based private sellers. Since October 2024, private sellers get 300 free listings a month with no final value fees. Fees only apply if you exceed 300 listings, add optional upgrades, or deliver to an overseas address.

faq.question: Is Vinted or eBay better for selling clothes?
faq.answer: For everyday and branded clothing, Vinted is usually better — its audience is fashion-focused, it's free with no listing cap, and integrated shipping handles postage. eBay is stronger for vintage, designer, collectible, and non-clothing items where its search-driven audience and courier flexibility help.

faq.question: Does Vinted or eBay charge more fees?
faq.answer: For casual UK private sellers, they're now roughly equal — both are free to list and sell. eBay caps free listings at 300 a month (then 35p each), while Vinted stays free regardless of volume. On Vinted the buyer pays a ~5% + £0.70 Buyer Protection fee; on eBay the buyer pays no visible protection fee.

faq.question: Which has better buyer protection, Vinted or eBay?
faq.answer: Both are solid. Vinted's Buyer Protection is a mandatory buyer-paid fee covering non-delivery, damage and not-as-described. eBay's Money Back Guarantee is free for buyers and covers the same situations. Both hold payment until delivery and side with buyers who provide good evidence.

faq.question: Can I sell the same item on Vinted and eBay?
faq.answer: Yes, and many resellers do — the audiences barely overlap, so cross-listing doubles your reach. The risk is selling the same item twice, so keep inventory in sync and delist immediately when something sells.
